summary: Post-2000 wave 3. Four postcolonial and science-studies person entries gain their later careers, debates and fuller cores, with read evidence. Dipesh Chakrabarty gains the climate work after 2009 (Tanner Lectures 2015; The Climate of History in a Planetary Age 2021), his critiques of the global frame and Big History and of the human/natural divide of Croce and Collingwood, the criticisms of Malm and Hornborg, LeCain and Staley, The Calling of History (2015), and later reception of Provincializing Europe. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak gains Death of a Discipline (2003) and its reviewers, “Righting Wrongs” (2004), the 2014 exchange with Chibber, two historians’ critiques (Eaton 2000, Moran 2014), the Kyoto (2012) and Holberg (2025) prizes, and a person-to-person critique of Guha (1985–88). Ranajit Guha gains History at the Limit of World-History (2002), Chibber’s critique of Dominance without Hegemony and its readers (2013–14), A Rule of Property for Bengal through Bhambra (2024), and readings to his obituaries (2023–24). Bruno Latour gains his Tarde critique of Durkheim (2002), An Inquiry into Modes of Existence (2012–13), Chakrabarty’s influence and their exchange (2013–20), Science in Action through Pickering (1994), and the Holberg (2013) and Kyoto (2021) prizes. Unread books are attributed to named readers.

rationale: The four entries stopped at 2009 (Chakrabarty, one point after 2000), 1999 (Spivak), 1989 (Guha) and 1999 (Latour), with two to four chronology points each. Every new edge rests on the person’s own words or a named reader’s explicit statement, read in full or in part with pages; abstract-only, metadata-only and prize-citation readings are labelled, and unread books are attributed locally to their reviewers. No new edge repeats an existing endpoint/type combination; later work that would have duplicated an arrow (Chakrabarty → environment; Spivak → subaltern) goes into edge revisions instead. Named critics without nodes are drawn through group entries with the critic named in the text (Chibber via historicalsociology; Malm, Hornborg and LeCain via environment; Staley via science; Eaton and Moran via truthdebate). Six edge revisions are made without retargeting: edge_914, edge_916 and edge_918 (Chakrabarty), edge_983 and edge_984 (Spivak), and edge_134 (Latour → sts). Three people records are added (vivek_chibber, richard_m_eaton, arik_moran). An Indigenous-history critique arrow for Ackerly, a Spivak → subaltern contribution parallel to edge_984, and Latour arrows to environment and historicism are left out (see release/README.md).

edge_914.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History', Representations 37 (1992), pp. 1–26, read in full (spacing restored in quotations): 'insofar as the academic discourse of history—that is, “history” as a discourse produced at the institutional site of the university—is concerned, “Europe” remains the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan,” and so on'; '“Indian” history itself is in a position of subalternity'; 'Europe' and 'India' are 'treated here as hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (p. 1). 'That Europe works as a silent referent in historical knowledge itself becomes obvious in a highly ordinary way': 'Third-world historians feel a need to refer to works in European history; historians of Europe do not feel any need to reciprocate' (p. 2). The everyday paradox is that 'we find these theories, in spite of their inherent ignorance of “us,” eminently useful in understanding our societies' (p. 3). 'Let us call this the project of provincializing “Europe”' (p. 20); it 'does not call for a simplistic, out-of-hand rejection of modernity, liberal values, universals, science, reason, grand narratives, totalizing explanations' (p. 20), and 'must realize within itself its own impossibility' (p. 22). Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 3–23 read in the publisher's excerpt: historicism 'made modernity or capitalism look ... as something that became global over time, by originating in one place (Europe) and then spreading outside it. This “first in Europe, then elsewhere” structure of global historical time was historicist' (p. 7); it 'came to non-European peoples in the nineteenth century as somebody's way of saying “not yet” to somebody else', and Mill's argument 'consigned Indians, Africans, and other “rude” nations to an imaginary waiting room of history' (p. 8). European thought 'is both indispensable and inadequate', and 'this simultaneous indispensability and inadequacy of social science thought is the task this book has set itself' (p. 6); 'provincializing Europe is not a project of rejecting or discarding European thought' (p. 16). The problem of capitalist modernity is 'a problem of translation, as well' as of transition (p. 17). Chapter 1 'reproduces, in an abridged form, a programmatic statement ... that I published in 1992 in the journal Representations' (p. 19). In-period reception and criticism: Arif Dirlik (Critical Inquiry 20, 1994; read) cites the 1992 essay (p. 334, n. 7) for postcolonial criticism's repudiation of the modes-of-production narrative, and objects that 'The denial of capitalism's foundational status also reveals a culturalism in the postcolonialist argument': 'Without capitalism as the foundation for European power and the motive force of its globalization, Eurocentrism would have been just another ethnocentrism' (p. 346). Dirlik's main target is Gyan Prakash; Chakrabarty appears only in his notes (nn. 7, 12). The wider in-period debate, not aimed at him by name: Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook, 'After Orientalism: Culture, Criticism, and Politics in the Third World', Comparative Studies in Society and History 34:1 (1992), pp. 141–167. The body is closed access; only the publisher's first-page extract and the article's notes (as listed on Cambridge Core) were read. The extract calls Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history, directions 'most recently and sharply endorsed in Gyan Prakash's discussion' (p. 141); a note objects that 'Prakash's notion of what constitutes Marxist history is problematic' (n. 13). None of the notes cites Chakrabarty. The 1.132 adversarial review, in a reading not checked here, summarises their case as doubting that the post-foundational programme can sustain historical explanation and political agency, and as holding that Marxist and social historians had already historicised their categories. Prakash replied in the same issue (pp. 168–184). This is criticism of the wider programme, principally Prakash's; it is not evidence of a criticism of Chakrabarty. A contribution, not a founding: the book's epigraph takes 'provincialized' from Gadamer (p. 3), and the post entry already maps Said and Spivak; his argument 'follows directly from my involvement' in Subaltern Studies (p. 15). edge_096 (post → modern) and edge_124 (post → global) stay: they record the group's critiques, which already name him. Later reception, added in revision 1.151 and dated after 2000: the 2007 edition is "Now featuring a new preface in which Chakrabarty responds to his critics" (publisher's page; the preface is unread), and Christopher Hill (Práticas da História, 2020, read in full) reports its claim that globalization was the project's "condition of possibility" (p. 55). Carola Dietze (History and Theory, 2008; abstract only) argues that he "has to be regarded as a thinker of radical historicism rather than as a critic of the discipline of history"; his reply (abstract only) finds "a degree of misapprehension". William H. Sewell Jr. (JWSR, 2014, read in full) writes that "Chakrabarty constructs a 'Marxism' fused with a hyperreal 'Europe' ... and then proceeds to criticize this construct", and "I prefer Chibber's version of the two histories to Chakrabarty's" (p. 302). The symposium divided over this reading: Bruce Cumings (JWSR, 2014, read in part), who says in the same passage that he does not know Guha's work, calls Chibber's account "a preposterous caricature of Chakrabarty's scholarship" (p. 292). Neither reader stands for the symposium as a whole. At the book's twentieth anniversary, Hill finds "ambiguities and contradictions" that are also "the source of its wide impact" (p. 53), and Bo Stråth (read in part) calls it "an immediate success" that "opened up a planetary perspective" (pp. 226, 229).

edge_916.evidence_note: His own statement of the book's aim. Rethinking Working-Class History (1989), preface pp. xi–xv and introduction pp. 3–6, read in the publisher preview (imprint: copyright 1989; first paperback printing 2000; preface dated February 1988): 'In looking at this history in terms of Marx's categories, however, my objective is to develop a critical understanding of these categories themselves'; 'there is an assumption regarding “culture” built into Marx's category of “capital,” and much of what I have to say on Indian labor history, and labor history in general, follows from this reading of Marx' (p. xi); 'this book is an extended polemic against the reductionism' of political-economic analysis of culture, the 'common sense' of Marxist labour history in India; 'Culture, one might say, is the “unthought” of Indian Marxism' (p. xii). 'Perhaps we have long overestimated capitalism's need or capacity to homogenize the cultural conditions necessary for its own reproduction' (p. xiii). He keeps a commitment to equality: 'The struggle to be a “citizen” must be part of the struggle to be a “comrade”' (p. xiv). The figure of the worker in Marx 'was that of a person who belonged to a society where the bourgeois notion of equality was ingrained in culture' (p. 3), and 'there is no “working class” or “working-class consciousness” that ... “is either transcendental in relation to the field of events or runs in its empty sameness throughout the course of history”' (p. 6, quoting Foucault). He separates his argument from Thompson's: 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5, n. 9). In-period reception by labour historians: Janaki Nair's review in International Labor and Working-Class History 37 (1990, pp. 96–99; not re-read here; the graph's verification note records that she recognises the theoretical contribution while questioning cultural determination, the treatment of traditions as survivals and the analysis of gender). Rajnarayan Chandavarkar, '“The Making of the Working Class”: E. P. Thompson and Indian History', History Workshop Journal 43 (1997; written for the 1994 History Workshop conference on Thompson; pp. 177–196 read): Thompson's 'inheritance' 'turned in Dipesh Chakrabarty's hands into a static, timeless, indeed Orientalist characterization of a “traditional” Indian, implicitly “Hindu” culture — in Bengal, a predominantly Muslim province' (p. 182); 'Bengali society, indeed Indian society, was now represented as England's proverbial Other' (p. 183); the view 'recently restated by Dipesh Chakrabarty, that rural migrants “imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting”' 'was not the product of an extensive investigation of the nature of labour migration' (pp. 184–185). Sarkar (1997, p. 87, page image checked) praises 'Dipesh Chakrabarty’s stimulating, if controversial, essays on Bengal labour history'; his n. 10 identifies them as the earlier Subaltern Studies essays 'Conditions for Knowledge of Working-Class Conditions: Employers, Government and the Jute-Workers of Calcutta, 1890–1940' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983) and 'Trade Unions in a Hierarchical Culture: The Jute Workers of Calcutta, 1920–50' (Subaltern Studies III, 1984), not the 1989 book. Nair (1990) and Chandavarkar (1997) are the in-period readings of the book itself. In 1992 he wrote that 'My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' of the transition narrative ('Artifice', p. 4). Context, not a genealogy: Eric Hobsbawm is among those he thanks for reading the manuscript (acknowledgments, p. xvii). edge_742 (subaltern → labourhistory) names him and Nair; see the proposed relabel. edge_358 (subaltern → social) stays. Added in revision 1.151, dated later: in a 2020 interview (read in full) he recalls that his Marxist teachers were uneasy at his evidence of Hindu–Muslim conflict among jute workers because, "as readers of E. P. Thompson, they assumed that there was a story waiting to be written about 'the making of the Indian working class'" (pp. 26–27); the paper became "Communal Riots and Labour" (Past and Present 91, 1981; unread). William H. Sewell Jr. (JWSR, 2014, read) reports that Chibber answers the 1989 book by showing that European and American capitalists "have repeatedly relied on personal authority and particularist identities" (p. 301; Chibber's book unread here), and prefers "Chibber's version of the two histories to Chakrabarty's" (p. 302); in the same symposium Bruce Cumings (read in part) calls Chibber's account "a preposterous caricature of Chakrabarty's scholarship" (p. 292), so the symposium did not agree on Chibber's reading.

edge_918.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009), developed into a distinction between globe and planet (2015–22)
edge_918.evidence_note: Dated 2009, after the atlas's 1920–2000 frame: drafted after the user's decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break. No claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) writes, tentatively, that the theses 'may prove more radical than even he intended, or perhaps desires' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here through their abstract, which holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis", and through his reports; the body of their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history. Later work, added in revision 1.151: the Tanner Lectures (2015, read in part) distinguish humanity as "homo" from the scientists' "anthropos" and conclude that "we have fallen into 'deep' history"; The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021; publisher's page and contents; unread) is summarised in his own words: "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 593). In environmental history's own journal, Atte Arffman (Environment and History, 2022, read) writes that "historians can no longer dismiss material realities and non-human world" and that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The criticisms of the species category and of the divide's novelty are now drawn separately (environment → Chakrabarty; science → Chakrabarty).

edge_983.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay. Later reception, added in revision 1.151: Interventions 4:2 (2002) devoted a special issue to A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, from a panel at the IAPL conference in 2000, with her response (metadata and abstracts only); Mark Sanders's abstract holds that placing "Can the subaltern speak?" in the book's "History" chapter "emphasizes its deconstruction of Marxist politics". Ritu Birla's abstract (the essay is unread) explores "the challenges of radical history writing" through the book's chapter on history, under the themes of "limits, the open secret, and value/transvaluation"; it sets Spivak beside Joan Scott's critique of "experience", opening "a discussion of the supplementary relationship of literature and history", and connects the limit of history to "the selective production of the archive".

edge_984.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88); the subaltern later reformulated as those 'removed from lines of social mobility' (2004)
edge_984.map_label: Strategic essentialism and the gendered subaltern, 1985–2004
edge_984.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79; this disagreement with Guha is drawn as its own person-to-person critique, Spivak → Guha, in this revision, and is no longer named in this edge's relationship); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. But the theoretically inclined metropolitan identitarians did’ (p. 332). Later reading, labelled: Partha Chatterjee (2010; Morris volume, unpaginated) recalls first reading both essays in 1985 with ‘bewilderment’ and calls her intervention ‘the poststructuralist moment in Subaltern Studies’, adding that a changed political context also drove the shift. A critique from within, not a rejection: she joined the editorial collective in the 1990s. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) carries the same story under the gender entry; see the proposed relabel. Guha’s person edge (pe137_guha_rel_01, guha draft) cites the same 1985 essay as reception; this edge is hers. Later reformulation and reading, added in revision 1.151 and dated after 2000: in "Righting Wrongs" (South Atlantic Quarterly, 2004; read in part, from a February 2001 lecture) she writes, "By subaltern I mean those removed from lines of social mobility" (p. 531), and warns that leaders from the domestic "below" ignore "the historically established discontinuity between themselves and the subaltern" (p. 535). Richard M. Eaton (Journal of World History, 2000, read p. 60) summarises the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians" for "positivist methodologies" (see the truthdebate critique).

edge_134.relationship: Laboratory ethnography (1979, with Woolgar) and the actor-network analysis of science and technology in the making (Science in Action, 1987)
edge_134.evidence_note: The author’s Laboratory Life record supports this contribution; no claim that Latour alone founded STS. Laboratory Life is coauthored with Steve Woolgar. Laboratory ethnography is a specified contribution, not Latour’s creation of all STS. Revision 1.151 adds two later judgements, attributed as such: Andrew Pickering (Modernism/modernity, 1994, read in full) called Science in Action (1987) "the most important book on science, technology and their intertwining with society published in the 1980s", whose actor-network analysis "flew in the face of technological and social determinist perspectives" (p. 257); the Holberg committee (2013) wrote that he "completely re-imagined Science Studies, pioneering new ethnographic methods" and that his work of the 1980s "established Actor Network Theory (ANT) as a widely used methodology". Science in Action is unread; Callon and Law are named as collaborators in the Kyoto citation.

text_revisions.old: A historian of modern South Asia in the Subaltern Studies collective. He argues that, within university-based historical discourse, an imagined 'Europe' remains its dominant theoretical reference: 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan”', where 'Europe' and 'India' are 'hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (1992). Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) reads Bengal’s jute-mill workers against an assumption of 'a hegemonic bourgeois culture' in Marx’s category of capital. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992) calls Europe 'a silent referent in historical knowledge', and Provincializing Europe (2000) criticises the historicist 'first in Europe, then elsewhere' that placed colonized peoples in 'an imaginary waiting room of history', while holding European thought 'both indispensable and inadequate'; a 2000 essay separates History 1, the past 'posited by capital', from History 2, pasts that are 'not pasts separate from capital' but 'inhere in capital and yet interrupt and punctuate' its logic. In period, Sumit Sarkar called the trajectory he described 'debilitating', and the labour historian Rajnarayan Chandavarkar found a 'static, timeless, indeed Orientalist' culture in his Bengal book. After 2000, 'The Climate of History' (2009) argued that climate change spells 'the collapse of the age-old humanist distinction between natural history and human history'.

Later readers of Provincializing Europe disputed it: Carola Dietze (2008, abstract only) regarded him as 'a thinker of radical historicism rather than as a critic of the discipline of history', and a 2014 symposium on Vivek Chibber’s critique divided: William Sewell found its 'Europe' a construct 'fused with' Marxism and preferred Chibber’s account, while Bruce Cumings called Chibber’s portrayal of Chakrabarty 'a preposterous caricature'; at its twentieth anniversary Christopher Hill found 'ambiguities and contradictions' in it that were also 'the source of its wide impact' (2020). After 2000 he turned to climate. 'The Climate of History' (2009) argued that climate change spells 'the collapse of the age-old humanist distinction between natural history and human history', a distinction he later traced 'from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood'. His Tanner Lectures (2015) questioned Big History's hope that large-scale history yields 'global citizenship', and The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021) sets the planet beside the globe: 'The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human' (2022). He also took up a long exchange with Bruno Latour (2013–20). Critics answered from several sides: Malm and Hornborg (2014), whose abstract (the article is unread) questions the 'species' category, holding inequalities within humanity 'part and parcel of the current ecological crisis' (that they address him is his own report); the environmental historian Timothy LeCain (2016) and the historian of science Richard Staley (2024) on the novelty of the divide; the political theorist Brooke Ackerly (2022) on his use of Indigenous histories, which she called 'dismissive and extractive'. Answering her, he grants that 'there is room for a deeper engagement with Indigenous traditions' while defending the meaning he gives Earth System Science, whose 'earth system' is 'my category “planet”', as no dismissal of 'other traditions and forms of planetary thought'; on capitalism he answers that capital and empire are 'a necessary but insufficient framework' (2022). The Calling of History (2015) studies the colonial historian Jadunath Sarkar and what a reviewer, Girija Joshi, calls the question of when a society values the 'objectivity' of historical research.

text_revisions.old: A literary theorist and the translator of Derrida’s Of Grammatology (1976), whose essays on colonial India became reference points for historians. In ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ (1985) she read the collective ‘from within but against the grain’, proposing that its recovery of subaltern consciousness be read ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’, and argued that it overlooked ‘how important the concept-metaphor woman is’ to its own discourse. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988) separates representation as ‘speaking for’ from ‘re-presentation’, argues that in Foucault and Deleuze’s conversation intellectuals, ‘representing them, ... represent themselves as transparent’, and reads the British abolition of sati through the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, set against the nativist ‘The women actually wanted to die’: between them ‘One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness.’ She later called the essay’s closing ‘the subaltern cannot speak!’ ‘an inadvisable remark’ (1999). In period, Gyan Prakash (1992) held that she ‘very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman’ as a limit of historical understanding, Rosalind O’Hanlon (1988) urged hesitation ‘before accepting’ her proposal to re-inscribe the series’ strategy ‘as a strategy for our times’, and Terry Eagleton (1999), crediting the book with addressing ‘the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’, found her Critique ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ and ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’.

text_revisions.old: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'.

Michael welcomed the turn to everyday life but warned that “losing sight of the state ... might mean the loss of it as an object of critique”; he also found the argument “mostly confined to the conceptual level”, without showing how Hegel’s ideas became colonial practice (2004). Dipesh Chakrabarty later called the book “his farewell to the discipline of history”, after which Guha wrote in Bengali (2024). Vivek Chibber’s Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital (2013) made Dominance without Hegemony a central target, arguing that its contrast between Indian and European bourgeoisies rests on “a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions”; William Sewell agreed that Guha’s portrayal of the English and French revolutions was “standard-issue orthodox Marxism”, while Partha Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denied that Guha made claims about those revolutions at all (2013–14).

Laboratory ethnography offers a route into science studies that should not be collapsed into textual interpretation or into Bloor’s programme. The Pasteur study extends his inquiry into historical scientific change and distinguishes that analysis from an explanation by social forces alone. Bloor’s1999response contests the treatment of sociological explanation in the Pasteur case. Andrew Pickering called Science in Action (1987) “the most important book on science, technology and their intertwining with society published in the 1980s”, read We Have Never Been Modern (1991; English 1993) as an account of a modern constitution that purifies nature from society, and objected that it leaves no room for the specific histories of labour, gender, colonialism and empire (1994). After 2000 he turned against Durkheim, presenting Gabriel Tarde as the forefather of actor-network theory in a volume on new bearings in history and the social sciences (2002). In “Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?” (2004) he asked whether he had been wrong “to participate in the invention of this field known as science studies”, while refusing “to swear that I will never be a constructivist any more”. His published description of Reassembling the Social (2005) presents sociology as “the science of associations and not only as the science of the social”. In An Inquiry into Modes of Existence (2012; English 2013) he imagined an anthropologist who studies the Moderns’ own institutions while refusing to believe “what the West says about itself”. Politics of Nature (1999; English 2004) proposed new institutions for political ecology; reviewing it, Antony Puddephatt found original propositions despite “an overall lack of empirical rigor” (2004). In his Holberg lecture (2013) he took up Dipesh Chakrabarty’s proposal that the Earth has again become “an agent of history” and called it a common geostory; the two discussed philosophies of history in a joint conversation (2020). By his own published descriptions, Facing Gaia (2015; English 2017) uses Lovelock’s Gaia to “disentangle the ethical, political, theological, and scientific aspects of the now obsolete notion of Nature”, and Down to Earth (2017; English 2018) defines politics “as what leads toward the Earth and not toward the global or the national”. The Holberg committee wrote that his influence reached “history, art history, philosophy, anthropology, geography, theology, literature and legal studies” (2013); he received the Kyoto Prize in 2021. Science in Action, We Have Never Been Modern, Politics of Nature, Reassembling the Social, Facing Gaia and Down to Earth are unread here; their arguments are given as reviewers, the prize committees or his own published descriptions state them. No review of An Inquiry into Modes of Existence, Facing Gaia or Down to Earth was read, so the debates around his later work are not covered here.
